questions.q: What defines a black-box method according to this lesson?
options: A method that requires physical access to the GPU running the model
Any method that uses a neural network of more than one billion parameters
A method that treats the model purely as a function from inputs to outputs, drawing conclusions only from observed behavior without examining weights or activations
A method that can only be used on open-source models
questions.explain: Black-box methods, including RLHF, red-teaming, and behavioral evals, all work by varying inputs (or input-derived training signals) and observing outputs, never touching what happens internally.

questions.q: How does mechanistic interpretability's central question differ from a black-box method's central question?
options: Mechanistic interpretability only asks about training data, never about computation
There is no real difference; both ask exactly the same question
Black-box methods ask 'what does the model do'; mechanistic methods ask 'what computation produces what the model does'
Black-box methods can only be used during training, while mechanistic methods can only be used after deployment
questions.explain: The lesson draws this exact distinction: black-box methods characterize behavior, while mechanistic methods try to explain the internal computation that produces that behavior.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe probing classifiers as a hybrid or in-between case?
options: Because they require access to internal activations (mechanistic in that sense) but only test whether a concept is linearly decodable, not whether the model's circuits actually use it computationally
Because they are black-box methods that happen to use a lot of compute
Because they can only be trained on labeled image data
Because they were invented before either black-box or mechanistic methods existed
questions.explain: Probing requires internal access, which is mechanistic in flavor, but a probe trained separately from the model's own computation only shows decodability, not a full circuit-level explanation of how the model uses that information.

questions.q: What is the 'circuits' research agenda, as described in this lesson's reverse-engineering framing?
options: Treating a trained network like a compiled program without source code, and trying to reverse-engineer it into human-understandable computational pathways built from interpretable features
A method for compressing models to run on edge devices
A benchmark for comparing black-box eval scores across models
A plan to redesign transformer architectures from scratch
questions.explain: Olah and colleagues' framing treats the network as something to decompile back into readable logic, identifying circuits of interpretable features rather than leaving the computation opaque.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does a mature safety case draw on both black-box and mechanistic approaches rather than just one?
options: Because black-box and mechanistic methods always produce contradictory results that must be reconciled
Because regulators require exactly two independent testing methods by law

Because black-box methods give broad, scalable behavioral coverage while mechanistic methods give confidence that good behavior isn't just a surface-level coincidence — each answers a question the other cannot
Because mechanistic methods are always more accurate and black-box methods are only used when compute is unavailable
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues neither approach replaces the other: black-box methods scale and answer direct behavioral questions, while mechanistic methods are costlier but can explain why behavior holds up, which behavioral testing alone cannot establish.
